title: Blackstone's AI Data Center Deals Are Looking Shaky
source_used: Bloomberg Opinion column by Shuli Ren, read in full in the Livemint copy (Bloomberg page prefetch holds two paragraphs)
key_facts: Bloomberg Opinion column by Shuli Ren, 13 Oct 2026: private credit lenders are writing big cheques to AI data-centre operators, who may need as much as $30 billion per gigawatt of computing power.
Public investors are pushing back on 'neoclouds', companies that buy chips and lease computing power; Sydney-based Firmus Grid's IPO failed last week.
Blackstone owns 6.7% of Firmus, joined a $2 billion funding round in August at a valuation above $10.5 billion and led a $10 billion debt facility earlier.
On Tuesday, news broke that AirTrunk, acquired by Blackstone in 2024, is delaying a planned Singapore REIT IPO; it had considered a yield of about 6%, up from 5.5%.
CoreWeave is expected to make $7.6 billion EBITDA this year but is still bleeding free cash flow and plans capex of up to $39 billion.
Chips are on a three- to six-year depreciation schedule, so neoclouds may have to book impairments if the chips lose relevance quickly.
AirTrunk and Lambda, another Blackstone investment, plan to go public in 2027; the column concludes the $1.3 trillion manager's AI data-centre deals are looking shaky.
quote_evidence: Public investors are now pushing back, asking whether AI data center developers can generate much shareholder value at all.
On Tuesday, news broke that the Australian data center operator is delaying a planned IPO of a real estate investment trust in Singapore.
Given how fast sentiments are turning, the $1.3 trillion asset manager's AI data center deals are looking shaky.
why_it_matters_hint: Cooling stock-market appetite for AI data-centre firms could leave lenders and Blackstone holding stakes they cannot sell at the hoped-for price.
notes: Opinion column. Bloomberg page prefetch holds two paragraphs; the full column was read in the Livemint copy (Bloomberg Opinion syndication). The column calls Firmus' failed IPO a '$30 billion' offering and later a '$30 billion ask' set against a valuation two months earlier; Reuters (C07-01) says Firmus shelved a $5 billion IPO. The figure is therefore left out of the summary.
